compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
Align the conditions before reading: the same matter, the same information, the same deadline and budget. If one is the person mainly responsible, duty will cover both columns and the preference becomes invisible.

Each row is written as a shared task with the basis each may attend to, and states which axis the row illustrates. Both types can use the other column; the table records only which is taken first more often.

| Shared task (one situation, one set of information) | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The household is about to spend a large sum | Apply the same budget and approval criteria to all options | Weigh how the same options would affect each family member’s everyday needs | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

| The plan is disrupted at short notice | Weigh feasible replacements against the same delivery criteria | Weigh which of those same replacements best honours commitments to the people affected | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F; both lean J, differing in what they protect when rearranging |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Either person might keep receipts, handle paperwork or follow up with a contractor. Those tasks reflect what the household needs and who has the experience and time to help.

The resemblance comes from the shared S and J. Both trust what can be checked: quotations, last year's receipts, who said what and when. Facing outer matters, both prefer to settle an arrangement rather than leave it hanging. Those two describe sourcing and stance only; they do not show who is more reliable, and do not mean either will necessarily finish the job.

The two differing axes are read separately. E/I compares where attention and energy flow more naturally — outward contact, discussion and pushing things along, or inner sorting, recalling and judging. T/F compares what judgement leans on — a standard that can be applied consistently, or the weight of people and values. Each axis stands alone and cannot substitute for the other.

### Signing off a sum: set the ceiling first, or ask who uses it daily

In this fictional renovation, both people have the same budget, deadline and information about how the household uses the space.

One may lay out the total, the amounts for each part of the project and how to handle overruns: keep ten per cent in reserve, stop one item when it is exceeded, and let the signatory carry responsibility. The gain is an executable frame within a short time; the cost is that items which are inconspicuous but used every day get pushed to the minimum, because their value is harder to capture in a budget summary.

The other may first ask how the days are actually lived: does the older relative need a night light for getting up, where does the child's desk move to, where do wet towels hang. The gain is that the money more likely lands where hands touch it daily; the cost is that the list grows with every question, and someone still has to cut it.

In comparing the two, what is worth looking at is not how the spreadsheet is written but what each side protected and what it gave up. Which item appears on paper first is rewritten by experience: anyone who has settled construction accounts, of either type, having been burned by an overrun, is more likely to nail the ceiling down first; where an older relative has bad knees, someone who normally sets the ceiling first will move money from the feature wall to the bathroom.

An easy method is for each to write one sheet, "cannot move" on the left and "can be cut" on the right, then swap and look. The purpose is not to detect a type but to bring the disagreement down to specific items — the two sheets usually overlap, and the overlap is what needs discussing.

### Why Si and Ne are shared while both judging functions change

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFJ is Si–Fe–Ti–Ne. Both have Si and Ne, only in different seats: ESTJ has Si second and Ne third; ISFJ has Si dominant and Ne fourth. What changes is the judging pair, Te and Fi against Fe and Ti.

That explains a pairing inside the model, not a process in real life. Both may remember a great deal of concrete detail; the model only says those details are usually fed into different stages: in the ESTJ arrangement Si sits next to the dominant Te, so detail more often supports standards and execution; in the ISFJ arrangement Si is itself dominant, so detail more often forms the baseline of "how this thing actually is". Neither statement shows who moves first, nor who has the better memory.

The two have different outward faces in the model: ESTJ turns its judging process outward as dominant Te, while ISFJ leads with the inward Si and judges outward through auxiliary Fe. Those are function positions in the model, not the order of actions in a room.

This page uses one common four-function notation, with the third position marked Ne and Ti respectively; sources differ on the introverted or extraverted attitude of the third process, and not all of them mark an attitude at all, so this writing should not be taken as the Foundation's unified notation. When a version disagrees, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair. Base descriptions are in the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [ISFJ profile](/en/personality/isfj).

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions, used to illustrate possible trade-offs, not to decide who suits which post or who should give way in a relationship. The division of work follows experience, how much information each holds and what each is willing to do, not type.

When the two work together, the usual misalignment is not about who is more capable but about one having built the frame while the other is still filling in detail. That is mostly solvable by process: who drafts first, who fills which section, who to ask when it sticks — none of it needs to become a question of character.

### Replacing office chairs: fix the budget first, or ask who is uncomfortable

(Fictional scene.) Administration has to replace thirty chairs in the open-plan area, the budget allows 600 yuan per chair, and the moving date is set. The same task, the same budget, two ways of preparing.

One may fix three things first — the unit price ceiling, the delivery date and the acceptance standard — then shortlist two suppliers from the comparison sheet and negotiate. The other may ask around privately first: who sits ten hours a day, who has a bad back and needs lumbar support, then arrange models by person and submit the budget.

The first gets the process through faster, at the risk of buying a height that does not suit, with returns going back through approval; the second gets people sitting comfortably, at the risk of having to reassemble quotations for three models and a harder delivery date. Both costs are real, and which is chosen depends on what this round fears more: delay, or returns.

Keep the counterexamples: anyone who has been dragged through two months of returns, of either type, will write the acceptance standard in detail; someone racing a move date will go down the list asking person by person. Experience and deadline change the approach; that is a condition, not a preference.

A workable check is for each to add one line on the back of the requirements sheet: "if only one thing can be met, which do I protect". If the answers are "delivery on time" and "lumbar support for everyone", the disagreement sits on two negotiable items and a compromise can be discussed; who leads the negotiation depends on who knows the suppliers and the approval process better.

### Who decides the renovation budget

(Fictional scene.) The answer is: whoever signs decides, and that follows authority and duty, not type. Either may take the lead; the difference is only which side is weighed first when doing so.

Move to the scene where the overrun has already happened: the original quote was 120,000 yuan, and the plumbing and electrical work is 18,000 yuan over budget, and the site manager wants a decision within three days. Both hold the same variation order and the same total gap.

One trade-off protects safety and high-frequency items first — plumbing, waterproofing, grab rails, night lights — postpones the feature wall and the second bedroom's dropped ceiling, and closes the gap by cutting non-essential items. The other tries to stay within the total by deferring optional work and spreading cuts across the remaining discretionary items. Both must keep the same safety requirements. The first may leave the visible result flat and awkward to account for at handover; the second may push daily-use items to the minimum and cost more to redo later.

To move this forward, three things have to be separated: whoever holds the quotation detail supplies the breakdown and variations, whoever has signing authority confirms, and the two agree a figure above which they reconsider together — written into the contract, not remembered. The reconsideration looks at the same variation order, not at anyone's attitude.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is taking E and I as "likes to run things" and "does not like to talk". ISFJ can be the one who organises everything in the family group — booking the restaurant, tracking the headcount; ESTJ can also sit alone with the bills for an afternoon. E/I describes where attention and energy flow more naturally, not how often someone socialises, and not who can carry more.

The second is taking T and F as "cold" and "warm". T/F measures neither warmth nor arithmetic ability; people of both preferences can hold a position, work the numbers and look after others. Using "who is colder" as evidence usually reads someone's expressive habit and how tired they are that day.

The third is ranking the two trade-offs. Putting the standard first saves rework; putting daily use first saves regret. Once ranked, the discussion slides from "how should this money be cut" to "who loves this family more".

The fourth is treating the first row of the budget sheet or the heading of a list as a criterion. How a sheet is written is shaped by templates, approval requirements and the format the last person left behind; the same type can produce completely different headings, and two identical-looking sheets can come from two entirely different considerations.

(Fictional scene.) Administration has to replace thirty chairs in the open-plan area, the budget allows 600 yuan per chair, and the moving date is set. The same task, the same budget, two ways of preparing.

One may fix three things first — the unit price ceiling, the delivery date and the acceptance standard — then shortlist two suppliers from the comparison sheet and negotiate. The other may ask around privately first: who sits ten hours a day, who has a bad back and needs lumbar support, then arrange models by person and submit the budget.

The first gets the process through faster, at the risk of buying a height that does not suit, with returns going back through approval; the second gets people sitting comfortably, at the risk of having to reassemble quotations for three models and a harder delivery date. Both costs are real, and which is chosen depends on what this round fears more: delay, or returns.

Keep the counterexamples: anyone who has been dragged through two months of returns, of either type, will write the acceptance standard in detail; someone racing a move date will go down the list asking person by person. faq_blocks.answer:
In the function position, not in proficiency: in the four-function notation used here, ESTJ's Si sits second, next to the dominant Te, while ISFJ's Si is dominant with Fe auxiliary for outward judgement.

That is a pairing inside the model, and cannot be used to infer who does what first, what their motive is, or who has the better memory or the better head for figures. Both may pull out an old precedent, and both may skip it — whether a precedent still applies depends on how far the conditions differ this time. faq_blocks.question: Both use Si — where does the difference show?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes, and commonly. Signing off and caring are learnable actions, on a different level from four letters.

Some ISFJs have cut a site manager's quote by ten per cent, and some ESTJs remember every worker's food restrictions. Neither shows a type, only experience and what someone cares about. To tell them apart, look not at who speaks first but at the reason: across comparable situations, do you hold the standard first, or look first at who has been left out. A reason is steadier than an action, but it still needs several situations.
faq_blocks.question: ISFJ also signs off, and ESTJ also looks after people?

faq_blocks.answer:
Not by type, but by experience, how much information each holds and what each wants to do. Whoever knows quotations and the sequence of works handles the budget part; whoever knows each family member's daily routine handles the usage detail; signing authority follows the household agreement or the contract.

A steadier approach splits the decision in two and agrees a figure above which they must talk again, written down rather than remembered. Then the argument is not about who decides but about which part each should speak to. If one person clearly does not want to handle money, assigning it by type only stalls the process.
faq_blocks.question: For a renovation, who is better at taking the lead?

faq_blocks.answer:
Most often on rhythm: when one wants to lock the budget and the other wants to complete the requirements first, two sentences appear — "the money is already decided and you are still asking" and "you signed before anyone had been asked".

A workable agreement is to spend the first ten minutes before work on one thing only: write three items each under "cannot move" and "can be cut", and stick them in one place. When it escalates, look at that sheet and change "you do not care about this family" into "should this line move to the can-be-cut column". The sheet is not a typing tool; it lays two people's trade-offs on one surface.

faq_blocks.answer:

summary_blocks.body:
ESTJ and ISFJ share S and J, and differ on E/I and T/F.

- S (Sensing): information more often trusts checkable facts and past experience, rather than abstract pattern and possibility first. This is shared.
- J (Judging): facing outer matters, both prefer structure and a clear arrangement rather than leaving options open. This is shared too, but it describes preference, not whether either actually finishes the work.
- E/I: whether attention and energy turn more naturally to outward interaction with people (E), or to the inner world and one's own sorting (I). This is direction, not how much someone talks, and not who organises things.
- T/F: whether judgement leans on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently (T), or counts people and values in as well (F).

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Te–Si–Ne–Fi for ESTJ and Si–Fe–Ti–Ne for ISFJ. The two share Si and Ne, while the judging pair becomes Te/Fi against Fe/Ti; the attitude of the third process is labelled differently elsewhere, and this writing is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These are emphases in the model. They do not predict order, and do not predict who should do what. With the same budget, either may set a ceiling first, and either may ask how it will be used first; which comes first depends more on role, experience, deadline and how much information is already in hand.

sections.title: Quick answer

body: Either person might keep receipts, handle paperwork or follow up with a contractor. Those tasks reflect what the household needs and who has the experience and time to help.

The resemblance comes from the shared S and J. Both trust what can be checked: quotations, last year's receipts, who said what and when. Facing outer matters, both prefer to settle an arrangement rather than leave it hanging. Those two describe sourcing and stance only; they do not show who is more reliable, and do not mean either will necessarily finish the job.

The two differing axes are read separately. E/I compares where attention and energy flow more naturally — outward contact, discussion and pushing things along, or inner sorting, recalling and judging. T/F compares what judgement leans on — a standard that can be applied consistently, or the weight of people and values. Each axis stands alone and cannot substitute for the other.
### Signing off a sum: set the ceiling first, or ask who uses it daily
In this fictional renovation, both people have the same budget, deadline and information about how the household uses the space.

One may lay out the total, the amounts for each part of the project and how to handle overruns: keep ten per cent in reserve, stop one item when it is exceeded, and let the signatory carry responsibility. The gain is an executable frame within a short time; the cost is that items which are inconspicuous but used every day get pushed to the minimum, because their value is harder to capture in a budget summary.

The other may first ask how the days are actually lived: does the older relative need a night light for getting up, where does the child's desk move to, where do wet towels hang. The gain is that the money more likely lands where hands touch it daily; the cost is that the list grows with every question, and someone still has to cut it.

In comparing the two, what is worth looking at is not how the spreadsheet is written but what each side protected and what it gave up. Which item appears on paper first is rewritten by experience: anyone who has settled construction accounts, of either type, having been burned by an overrun, is more likely to nail the ceiling down first; where an older relative has bad knees, someone who normally sets the ceiling first will move money from the feature wall to the bathroom.

An easy method is for each to write one sheet, "cannot move" on the left and "can be cut" on the right, then swap and look. The purpose is not to detect a type but to bring the disagreement down to specific items — the two sheets usually overlap, and the overlap is what needs discussing.
### Why Si and Ne are shared while both judging functions change

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFJ is Si–Fe–Ti–Ne. Both have Si and Ne, only in different seats: ESTJ has Si second and Ne third; ISFJ has Si dominant and Ne fourth. What changes is the judging pair, Te and Fi against Fe and Ti.

That explains a pairing inside the model, not a process in real life. Both may remember a great deal of concrete detail; the model only says those details are usually fed into different stages: in the ESTJ arrangement Si sits next to the dominant Te, so detail more often supports standards and execution; in the ISFJ arrangement Si is itself dominant, so detail more often forms the baseline of "how this thing actually is". Neither statement shows who moves first, nor who has the better memory.

The two have different outward faces in the model: ESTJ turns its judging process outward as dominant Te, while ISFJ leads with the inward Si and judges outward through auxiliary Fe. Those are function positions in the model, not the order of actions in a room.

This page uses one common four-function notation, with the third position marked Ne and Ti respectively; sources differ on the introverted or extraverted attitude of the third process, and not all of them mark an attitude at all, so this writing should not be taken as the Foundation's unified notation. When a version disagrees, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair. Base descriptions are in the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [ISFJ profile](/en/personality/isfj).

body: Align the conditions before reading: the same matter, the same information, the same deadline and budget. If one is the person mainly responsible, duty will cover both columns and the preference becomes invisible.

Each row is written as a shared task with the basis each may attend to, and states which axis the row illustrates. Both types can use the other column; the table records only which is taken first more often.

| Shared task (one situation, one set of information) | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The household is about to spend a large sum | Apply the same budget and approval criteria to all options | Weigh how the same options would affect each family member’s everyday needs | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Someone disagrees face to face | Whether this conflicts with the standard already set | Whether the person raising it was heard and will not be left out | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The plan is disrupted at short notice | Weigh feasible replacements against the same delivery criteria | Weigh which of those same replacements best honours commitments to the people affected | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F; both lean J, differing in what they protect when rearranging |
| Something extra lands on a Friday evening | May find it easier to understand the same request by talking it through | May find it easier to understand the same request by reflecting privately | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Sitting among relatives you hardly know | Work out the rules and the seating of the occasion first | Notice first who is most uncomfortable, and whether to say a word | Occasion arrangement and how those present feel; both may attend |
| Looking back a year later | Judge whether the outcome met the same criteria agreed at the start | Judge how the outcome affected the people who helped and those using the result | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

The shared S shows in both columns landing on concrete facts: neither talks only in abstract principles. The T/F rows compare criteria for decisions. The E/I row compares how someone works through the same request. The differences in the table are not a scale of ability or a ranking of proficiency; the same person reaches both columns under different duties and amounts of information.

body: Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions, used to illustrate possible trade-offs, not to decide who suits which post or who should give way in a relationship. The division of work follows experience, how much information each holds and what each is willing to do, not type.

When the two work together, the usual misalignment is not about who is more capable but about one having built the frame while the other is still filling in detail. That is mostly solvable by process: who drafts first, who fills which section, who to ask when it sticks — none of it needs to become a question of character.
### Replacing office chairs: fix the budget first, or ask who is uncomfortable

(Fictional scene.) Administration has to replace thirty chairs in the open-plan area, the budget allows 600 yuan per chair, and the moving date is set. The same task, the same budget, two ways of preparing.

One may fix three things first — the unit price ceiling, the delivery date and the acceptance standard — then shortlist two suppliers from the comparison sheet and negotiate. The other may ask around privately first: who sits ten hours a day, who has a bad back and needs lumbar support, then arrange models by person and submit the budget.

The first gets the process through faster, at the risk of buying a height that does not suit, with returns going back through approval; the second gets people sitting comfortably, at the risk of having to reassemble quotations for three models and a harder delivery date. Both costs are real, and which is chosen depends on what this round fears more: delay, or returns.

Keep the counterexamples: anyone who has been dragged through two months of returns, of either type, will write the acceptance standard in detail; someone racing a move date will go down the list asking person by person. Experience and deadline change the approach; that is a condition, not a preference.

A workable check is for each to add one line on the back of the requirements sheet: "if only one thing can be met, which do I protect". If the answers are "delivery on time" and "lumbar support for everyone", the disagreement sits on two negotiable items and a compromise can be discussed; who leads the negotiation depends on who knows the suppliers and the approval process better.
### Who decides the renovation budget
(Fictional scene.) The answer is: whoever signs decides, and that follows authority and duty, not type. Either may take the lead; the difference is only which side is weighed first when doing so.

Move to the scene where the overrun has already happened: the original quote was 120,000 yuan, and the plumbing and electrical work is 18,000 yuan over budget, and the site manager wants a decision within three days. Both hold the same variation order and the same total gap.

One trade-off protects safety and high-frequency items first — plumbing, waterproofing, grab rails, night lights — postpones the feature wall and the second bedroom's dropped ceiling, and closes the gap by cutting non-essential items. The other tries to stay within the total by deferring optional work and spreading cuts across the remaining discretionary items. Both must keep the same safety requirements. The first may leave the visible result flat and awkward to account for at handover; the second may push daily-use items to the minimum and cost more to redo later.

To move this forward, three things have to be separated: whoever holds the quotation detail supplies the breakdown and variations, whoever has signing authority confirms, and the two agree a figure above which they reconsider together — written into the contract, not remembered. The reconsideration looks at the same variation order, not at anyone's attitude.

body: The first misread is taking E and I as "likes to run things" and "does not like to talk". ISFJ can be the one who organises everything in the family group — booking the restaurant, tracking the headcount; ESTJ can also sit alone with the bills for an afternoon. E/I describes where attention and energy flow more naturally, not how often someone socialises, and not who can carry more.

The second is taking T and F as "cold" and "warm". T/F measures neither warmth nor arithmetic ability; people of both preferences can hold a position, work the numbers and look after others. Using "who is colder" as evidence usually reads someone's expressive habit and how tired they are that day.

The third is ranking the two trade-offs. Putting the standard first saves rework; putting daily use first saves regret. Once ranked, the discussion slides from "how should this money be cut" to "who loves this family more".

The fourth is treating the first row of the budget sheet or the heading of a list as a criterion. How a sheet is written is shaped by templates, approval requirements and the format the last person left behind; the same type can produce completely different headings, and two identical-looking sheets can come from two entirely different considerations.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring convention first, then which part of life you were referring to when answering: a project at work, or something at home. Item format and recent circumstances rewrite answers, so do not assume in advance which letter you will lean to.

The practice can be an open record, with no first item and no threshold on occasions. Next time the household is about to spend money, do not discuss it first; each writes three lines: what I least want to give up this time; what basis I used when there was a conflict; which constraints changed my choice.

After a few of these, look back — not at which line you wrote on, but at whether your trade-off changes when the same kind of constraint recurs. These records help you see the situation and your own weighing habit; they are not scored, do not assign a type, and a trend across a few records cannot replace an interpretation of the assessment result.

ESTJ and ISFJ share S and J, and differ on E/I and T/F.

- S (Sensing): information more often trusts checkable facts and past experience, rather than abstract pattern and possibility first. This is shared.
- J (Judging): facing outer matters, both prefer structure and a clear arrangement rather than leaving options open. This is shared too, but it describes preference, not whether either actually finishes the work.
- E/I: whether attention and energy turn more naturally to outward interaction with people (E), or to the inner world and one's own sorting (I). This is direction, not how much someone talks, and not who organises things.
- T/F: whether judgement leans on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently (T), or counts people and values in as well (F).

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Te–Si–Ne–Fi for ESTJ and Si–Fe–Ti–Ne for ISFJ. The two share Si and Ne, while the judging pair becomes Te/Fi against Fe/Ti; the attitude of the third process is labelled differently elsewhere, and this writing is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These are emphases in the model. They do not predict order, and do not predict who should do what. With the same budget, either may set a ceiling first, and either may ask how it will be used first; which comes first depends more on role, experience, deadline and how much information is already in hand.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Either person might keep receipts, handle paperwork or follow up with a contractor. Those tasks reflect what the household needs and who has the experience and time to help.

The resemblance comes from the shared S and J. Both trust what can be checked: quotations, last year's receipts, who said what and when. Facing outer matters, both prefer to settle an arrangement rather than leave it hanging. Those two describe sourcing and stance only; they do not show who is more reliable, and do not mean either will necessarily finish the job.

The two differing axes are read separately. E/I compares where attention and energy flow more naturally — outward contact, discussion and pushing things along, or inner sorting, recalling and judging. T/F compares what judgement leans on — a standard that can be applied consistently, or the weight of people and values. Each axis stands alone and cannot substitute for the other.

### Signing off a sum: set the ceiling first, or ask who uses it daily

In this fictional renovation, both people have the same budget, deadline and information about how the household uses the space.

One may lay out the total, the amounts for each part of the project and how to handle overruns: keep ten per cent in reserve, stop one item when it is exceeded, and let the signatory carry responsibility. The gain is an executable frame within a short time; the cost is that items which are inconspicuous but used every day get pushed to the minimum, because their value is harder to capture in a budget summary.

The other may first ask how the days are actually lived: does the older relative need a night light for getting up, where does the child's desk move to, where do wet towels hang. The gain is that the money more likely lands where hands touch it daily; the cost is that the list grows with every question, and someone still has to cut it.

In comparing the two, what is worth looking at is not how the spreadsheet is written but what each side protected and what it gave up. Which item appears on paper first is rewritten by experience: anyone who has settled construction accounts, of either type, having been burned by an overrun, is more likely to nail the ceiling down first; where an older relative has bad knees, someone who normally sets the ceiling first will move money from the feature wall to the bathroom.

An easy method is for each to write one sheet, "cannot move" on the left and "can be cut" on the right, then swap and look. The purpose is not to detect a type but to bring the disagreement down to specific items — the two sheets usually overlap, and the overlap is what needs discussing.

### Why Si and Ne are shared while both judging functions change

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFJ is Si–Fe–Ti–Ne. Both have Si and Ne, only in different seats: ESTJ has Si second and Ne third; ISFJ has Si dominant and Ne fourth. What changes is the judging pair, Te and Fi against Fe and Ti.

That explains a pairing inside the model, not a process in real life. Both may remember a great deal of concrete detail; the model only says those details are usually fed into different stages: in the ESTJ arrangement Si sits next to the dominant Te, so detail more often supports standards and execution; in the ISFJ arrangement Si is itself dominant, so detail more often forms the baseline of "how this thing actually is". Neither statement shows who moves first, nor who has the better memory.

The two have different outward faces in the model: ESTJ turns its judging process outward as dominant Te, while ISFJ leads with the inward Si and judges outward through auxiliary Fe. Those are function positions in the model, not the order of actions in a room.

This page uses one common four-function notation, with the third position marked Ne and Ti respectively; sources differ on the introverted or extraverted attitude of the third process, and not all of them mark an attitude at all, so this writing should not be taken as the Foundation's unified notation. When a version disagrees, check whether it states its source, then read the first two positions for this pair. Base descriptions are in the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [ISFJ profile](/en/personality/isfj).
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFJ: shared ground and the core difference

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions before reading: the same matter, the same information, the same deadline and budget. If one is the person mainly responsible, duty will cover both columns and the preference becomes invisible.

Each row is written as a shared task with the basis each may attend to, and states which axis the row illustrates. Both types can use the other column; the table records only which is taken first more often.

| Shared task (one situation, one set of information) | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The household is about to spend a large sum | Apply the same budget and approval criteria to all options | Weigh how the same options would affect each family member’s everyday needs | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Someone disagrees face to face | Whether this conflicts with the standard already set | Whether the person raising it was heard and will not be left out | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The plan is disrupted at short notice | Weigh feasible replacements against the same delivery criteria | Weigh which of those same replacements best honours commitments to the people affected | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F; both lean J, differing in what they protect when rearranging |
| Something extra lands on a Friday evening | May find it easier to understand the same request by talking it through | May find it easier to understand the same request by reflecting privately | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Sitting among relatives you hardly know | Work out the rules and the seating of the occasion first | Notice first who is most uncomfortable, and whether to say a word | Occasion arrangement and how those present feel; both may attend |
| Looking back a year later | Judge whether the outcome met the same criteria agreed at the start | Judge how the outcome affected the people who helped and those using the result | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

The shared S shows in both columns landing on concrete facts: neither talks only in abstract principles. The T/F rows compare criteria for decisions. The E/I row compares how someone works through the same request. The differences in the table are not a scale of ability or a ranking of proficiency; the same person reaches both columns under different duties and amounts of information.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions, used to illustrate possible trade-offs, not to decide who suits which post or who should give way in a relationship. The division of work follows experience, how much information each holds and what each is willing to do, not type.

When the two work together, the usual misalignment is not about who is more capable but about one having built the frame while the other is still filling in detail. That is mostly solvable by process: who drafts first, who fills which section, who to ask when it sticks — none of it needs to become a question of character.

### Replacing office chairs: fix the budget first, or ask who is uncomfortable

(Fictional scene.) Administration has to replace thirty chairs in the open-plan area, the budget allows 600 yuan per chair, and the moving date is set. The same task, the same budget, two ways of preparing.

One may fix three things first — the unit price ceiling, the delivery date and the acceptance standard — then shortlist two suppliers from the comparison sheet and negotiate. The other may ask around privately first: who sits ten hours a day, who has a bad back and needs lumbar support, then arrange models by person and submit the budget.

The first gets the process through faster, at the risk of buying a height that does not suit, with returns going back through approval; the second gets people sitting comfortably, at the risk of having to reassemble quotations for three models and a harder delivery date. Both costs are real, and which is chosen depends on what this round fears more: delay, or returns.

Keep the counterexamples: anyone who has been dragged through two months of returns, of either type, will write the acceptance standard in detail; someone racing a move date will go down the list asking person by person. Experience and deadline change the approach; that is a condition, not a preference.

A workable check is for each to add one line on the back of the requirements sheet: "if only one thing can be met, which do I protect". If the answers are "delivery on time" and "lumbar support for everyone", the disagreement sits on two negotiable items and a compromise can be discussed; who leads the negotiation depends on who knows the suppliers and the approval process better.

### Who decides the renovation budget

(Fictional scene.) The answer is: whoever signs decides, and that follows authority and duty, not type. Either may take the lead; the difference is only which side is weighed first when doing so.

Move to the scene where the overrun has already happened: the original quote was 120,000 yuan, and the plumbing and electrical work is 18,000 yuan over budget, and the site manager wants a decision within three days. Both hold the same variation order and the same total gap.

One trade-off protects safety and high-frequency items first — plumbing, waterproofing, grab rails, night lights — postpones the feature wall and the second bedroom's dropped ceiling, and closes the gap by cutting non-essential items. The other tries to stay within the total by deferring optional work and spreading cuts across the remaining discretionary items. Both must keep the same safety requirements. The first may leave the visible result flat and awkward to account for at handover; the second may push daily-use items to the minimum and cost more to redo later.

To move this forward, three things have to be separated: whoever holds the quotation detail supplies the breakdown and variations, whoever has signing authority confirms, and the two agree a figure above which they reconsider together — written into the contract, not remembered. The reconsideration looks at the same variation order, not at anyone's attitude.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The first misread is taking E and I as "likes to run things" and "does not like to talk". ISFJ can be the one who organises everything in the family group — booking the restaurant, tracking the headcount; ESTJ can also sit alone with the bills for an afternoon. E/I describes where attention and energy flow more naturally, not how often someone socialises, and not who can carry more.

The second is taking T and F as "cold" and "warm". T/F measures neither warmth nor arithmetic ability; people of both preferences can hold a position, work the numbers and look after others. Using "who is colder" as evidence usually reads someone's expressive habit and how tired they are that day.

The third is ranking the two trade-offs. Putting the standard first saves rework; putting daily use first saves regret. Once ranked, the discussion slides from "how should this money be cut" to "who loves this family more".

The fourth is treating the first row of the budget sheet or the heading of a list as a criterion. How a sheet is written is shaped by templates, approval requirements and the format the last person left behind; the same type can produce completely different headings, and two identical-looking sheets can come from two entirely different considerations.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring convention first, then which part of life you were referring to when answering: a project at work, or something at home. Item format and recent circumstances rewrite answers, so do not assume in advance which letter you will lean to.

The practice can be an open record, with no first item and no threshold on occasions. Next time the household is about to spend money, do not discuss it first; each writes three lines: what I least want to give up this time; what basis I used when there was a conflict; which constraints changed my choice.

After a few of these, look back — not at which line you wrote on, but at whether your trade-off changes when the same kind of constraint recurs. These records help you see the situation and your own weighing habit; they are not scored, do not assign a type, and a trend across a few records cannot replace an interpretation of the assessment result.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
E/I and T/F, and both differ at once: one compares whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more naturally, the other whether judgement leans on impersonal consistent criteria or on people and values.

So "who is more extraverted" cannot decide it. Both may organise a roomful of people when needed, and both may say nothing when tired. To explore E/I, compare where your attention goes when you can choose how to work through the same information. To explore T/F, ask whether you gave more weight to applying a consistent standard or to what a decision meant to the people affected. A single phrasing or a single sheet is not a criterion.
items.question: Which letters carry the difference?

items.answer:
In the function position, not in proficiency: in the four-function notation used here, ESTJ's Si sits second, next to the dominant Te, while ISFJ's Si is dominant with Fe auxiliary for outward judgement.

That is a pairing inside the model, and cannot be used to infer who does what first, what their motive is, or who has the better memory or the better head for figures. Both may pull out an old precedent, and both may skip it — whether a precedent still applies depends on how far the conditions differ this time. To understand yourself, reviewing which basis you cite in a few real decisions is more reliable than reading a function table.
items.question: Both use Si — where does the difference show?

items.answer:
Yes, and commonly. Signing off and caring are learnable actions, on a different level from four letters.

Some ISFJs have cut a site manager's quote by ten per cent, and some ESTJs remember every worker's food restrictions. Neither shows a type, only experience and what someone cares about. To tell them apart, look not at who speaks first but at the reason: across comparable situations, do you hold the standard first, or look first at who has been left out. A reason is steadier than an action, but it still needs several situations.
items.question: ISFJ also signs off, and ESTJ also looks after people?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by experience, how much information each holds and what each wants to do. Whoever knows quotations and the sequence of works handles the budget part; whoever knows each family member's daily routine handles the usage detail; signing authority follows the household agreement or the contract.

A steadier approach splits the decision in two and agrees a figure above which they must talk again, written down rather than remembered. Then the argument is not about who decides but about which part each should speak to. If one person clearly does not want to handle money, assigning it by type only stalls the process.
items.question: For a renovation, who is better at taking the lead?

items.answer:
Most often on rhythm: when one wants to lock the budget and the other wants to complete the requirements first, two sentences appear — "the money is already decided and you are still asking" and "you signed before anyone had been asked".

A workable agreement is to spend the first ten minutes before work on one thing only: write three items each under "cannot move" and "can be cut", and stick them in one place. When it escalates, look at that sheet and change "you do not care about this family" into "should this line move to the can-be-cut column". The sheet is not a typing tool; it lays two people's trade-offs on one surface.
items.question: Living together, where do ESTJ and ISFJ most often get stuck?

items.answer:
Do not choose between them yet; first confirm whether both used the same questionnaire, language version and scoring convention, then look at the E/I and T/F results separately.

If the tool provides interpretable dimension scores and both sit near the boundary, that only means this round landed near that tool's boundary, and does not directly imply a weak or unstable preference. Recall whether you were answering as the person at work or the person at home, and record that situation; do not assume in advance which letter the answer will lean to, and do not treat the household ledger as a retest validation.
